title: Default Options In Advance Directives Influence How Patients Set Goals For End-Of-Life Care
abstract: Although decisions regarding end-of-life care are personal and important, they may be influenced by the ways in which options are presented. To test this hypothesis, we randomly assigned 132 seriously ill patients to complete one of three types of advance directives. Two types had end-of-life care options already checked-a default choice-but one of these favored comfort-oriented care, and the other, life-extending care. The third type was a standard advance directive with no options checked. We found that most patients preferred comfort-oriented care, but the defaults influenced those choices. For example, 77 percent of patients in the comfort-oriented group retained that choice, while 43 percent of those in the life-extending group rejected the default choice and selected comfort-oriented care instead. Among the standard advance directive group, 61 percent of patients selected comfort-oriented care. Our findings suggest that patients may not hold deep-seated preferences regarding end-of-life care. The findings provide motivation for future research examining whether using default options in advance directives may improve important outcomes, including patients' receipt of wanted and unwanted services, resource use, survival, and quality of life.

claims.text: Most seriously ill patients prefer comfort-oriented care over life-extending care when completing advance directives.
Default options pre-selected in advance directives influence patients' end-of-life care choices.
Seventy-seven percent of patients assigned to an advance directive defaulting to comfort-oriented care retained that choice.
Forty-three percent of patients assigned to an advance directive defaulting to life-extending care rejected the default and chose comfort-oriented care.
Sixty-one percent of patients assigned to a standard advance directive with no pre-checked defaults selected comfort-oriented care.
Seriously ill patients may not hold deep-seated preferences regarding end-of-life care.

future_work.text: Examine whether using default options in advance directives improves outcomes such as receipt of wanted and unwanted services, resource use, survival, and quality of life.

methodologies.name: Randomized controlled trial of advance directive default options
methodologies.description: Randomized 132 seriously ill patients to complete one of three advance directive types: comfort-oriented care pre-checked, life-extending care pre-checked, or a standard form with no pre-checked options.
